The Piquitinga anchovy, Anchoa tricolor, is a small engraulid that supports important coastal fisheries along the southwestern Atlantic seaboard. Individuals hatched from eggs with a diameter of 1.2 mm produce a neonate with a dry tissue mass of only 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to the prolarva following chorion rupture. The yolk-sac larva, an endotrophic alevin measuring just a few millimeters, absorbs its endogenous nutrients within days under typical thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 22.6 °C [T = 22.6 °C], hatching occurs approximately six days [ab = approximately six days] after fertilization, a developmental duration consistent with estimates for the congeneric species Engraulis encrasicolus under similar thermal regimes. The postflexion larva then begins exogenous feeding upon yolk-sac resorption, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth in the pelagic zone. This early life stage is particularly vulnerable to starvation and predation, making the timing of the trophic switch critical for cohort survival. The species thus exhibits a classic r-selected reproductive strategy, with high fecundity and small offspring size, compensating for the modest individual investment per egg through substantial spawning output across the breeding season.

The timing of reproductive maturation in Anchoa tricolor is tightly linked to body size rather than age alone, with puberty being attained at a standard length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters]. At this size, an individual's wet mass averages 2.34 grams [Wwp = 2.34 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions specific to this species. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis marks the transition from the growing juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase, during which gonadal development becomes a significant metabolic investment. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for actively spawning individuals was measured at 5% [GSI = 5%] at a temperature of 22.6 °C [T = 22.6 °C]. This may reflect the species' batch-spawning strategy, in which oocytes are hydrated and released in multiple events over a protracted spawning period rather than as a single massive deposition. Consequently, while individual batch fecundity is relatively low, the cumulative seasonal output can be substantial, allowing the population to exploit ephemeral plankton blooms effectively.

Maximum body size in wild populations of Piquitinga anchovy is constrained by both physiological limits and ecological mortality, with the ultimate standard length reaching 14.9 centimeters [Li = 14.9 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the maximum recorded wet weight among adult teleosts in this species is 24.5 grams [Wwi = 24.5 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass approached as growth slows during the post-pubertal period. This relatively small maximum size is characteristic of short-lived, fast-growing coastal forage fish, which allocate energy predominantly to reproduction rather than continued somatic expansion after maturity. Large adults over 20 grams are uncommon in most samples, likely due to size-selective predation by piscivorous fish as well as fishing pressure. In Brazilian coastal waters, individuals exceeding this threshold are typically gravid females preparing to spawn, their body cavities filled with hydrated oocytes. The allometric relationship between length and weight follows a power function consistent with other engraulids, though local populations may exhibit subtle differences in condition factor depending on prey availability and water temperature.

Longevity estimates for Anchoa tricolor are derived from otolith-based age readings and mark-recapture studies, indicating a maximum lifespan of 876 days [am = 876 days] under sustained temperature conditions of 22.6 °C [T = 22.6 °C]. This two-and-a-half-year life expectancy places the species among the shorter-lived members of the Engraulidae, consistent with its rapid growth and early maturation schedule. Senescence is not well documented in wild schooling fish, but captive observations suggest that individuals beyond two years exhibit reduced condition and increased susceptibility to disease. The species likely experiences high natural mortality throughout life, with the majority of individuals failing to reach the upper age limit due to predation and fisheries exploitation. Seasonal temperature fluctuations may accelerate or decelerate the aging process, though the precise metabolic mechanisms remain unstudied. From a life-history perspective, a maximum span of 876 days limits the number of reproductive seasons available to any single individual, reinforcing the evolutionary pressure toward early and intense spawning effort. The population's resilience thus depends on consistent recruitment of young-of-year into the adult stock.

The reproductive schedule of Anchoa tricolor is characterized by iteroparity within its abbreviated lifespan, with batch spawning distributed across the warmest months of the year. At the species' preferred thermal regime of 22.6 °C [T = 22.6 °C], females mature rapidly and commence spawning within their first year of life. The age at first reproduction is estimated to fall within the early juvenile period, shortly after individuals reach the size threshold required for vitellogenesis onset. Field surveys have recorded gravid females as small as 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] standard length, indicating that reproductive investment begins almost immediately following sexual maturation. This accelerated schedule is typical of engraulids inhabiting productive upwelling systems, where high food availability supports the energetic demands of gamete production. The relatively small maximum body size of 14.9 centimeters [Li = 14.9 centimeters] limits the absolute volume of the peritoneal cavity available for ovary expansion, but multiple spawning events across the breeding season compensate by distributing fecundity over time. The population's spawning success is tightly coupled to oceanographic conditions that concentrate planktonic prey for the exogenously feeding larvae.
